Black-Hole Jets Reach Beyond Galaxies

A study of 324 galaxies has found evidence that powerful jets launched by supermassive black holes can energise gas far beyond their host galaxies, potentially affecting the material needed to form new stars.

The gas, known as the circumgalactic medium (CGM), can extend 10–20 times farther than a galaxy itself. It acts as a reservoir that can eventually supply material for star formation. Yet galaxies do not produce stars at the enormous rates that might be expected if all this gas cooled and collapsed.

Astronomers have long suspected that supermassive black holes could help prevent this cooling. The new study, led by Namrata Roy, Assistant Professor in the Astronomy and Astrophysics Division at the Raman Research Institute, provides observational evidence for one possible mechanism.

Black-Hole Jets Create a Powerful Signal

The researchers studied 324 galaxies whose central black holes launch powerful jets of hot, fast-moving plasma. Using data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), they searched for a faint red glow produced by ionised hydrogen in the CGM.

The gas was found to glow about 100 times brighter than in similar galaxies without such jets, particularly along the direction of the jets.

When the researchers averaged the gas in all directions around the galaxies, the signal disappeared. But when they focused on the areas aligned with the jets, a strong signal emerged.

The findings suggest the jets compress, heat and ionise the surrounding gas, acting more like a narrow beam than a source of energy spreading uniformly in every direction.

Where Jets Meet Circumgalactic Gas

The strongest signal appeared in two regions: near the edge of the galaxy’s stellar disk, where the jet first encounters the CGM, and near the outer boundary of the CGM, where the slowing jet deposits energy into the surrounding gas.

The researchers also examined magnesium as a tracer of cooler gas. Unlike the ionised gas, the cooler material was distributed more uniformly around the galaxies.

This suggests the jets do not create or remove the cooler gas across the CGM. Instead, they appear to energise the portion lying directly in their path.

Could Black-Hole Jets Affect Star Formation?

Cold gas can cool, clump and eventually form stars. By injecting energy into the gas, black-hole jets could make it harder for some of this material to cool and collapse efficiently.

However, the study does not yet prove that the jets directly suppress star formation. Instead, it shows that energy released by a black hole can reach gas hundreds of thousands of light-years away and alter its state.

The researchers say further observations and modelling are needed to establish whether galaxies more strongly affected by jets actually form fewer stars. They plan to study the glowing gas in individual galaxies using telescopes such as Hubble, measuring how quickly the gas moves and how it is energised.
